clue.text: Tramp pays pounds to move to the west

parts.note: someone who foots a bill pays it
L is the abbreviation for pounds sterling, from the Latin libra

indicators.note: in an across entry, heading west means running right to left, so the word for moving is written backwards

parts.note: to go is to move from one place to another

explanation.surface: A vagrant hands over money so that he can relocate westwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tramp' reads as a vagrant, but here it is the verb for trudging along on foot; 'to the west' turns only the final piece.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb, to tramp is to trudge wearily over a long distance, a synonym for marching on foot.

clue.text: Northern bloke in east end residence, an unfussy eater

indicators.note: in says the northern letter and the man's name sit inside the word for the residence

parts.note: a Cockney from London's East End drops the H, so home, a residence, is said without it
Ivor is a man's name, standing for a bloke

explanation.surface: A man from the north living in an East London house will eat anything.
explanation.walkthrough: London's East End is the home of Cockney speech, which drops the letter H at the start of words; 'in' then makes that clipped word the container.
explanation.definitionFit: An animal or person that eats every kind of food, plant or meat, is by description not picky about diet.

clue.text: Put up writer next to church for small cost

indicators.note: next to says the writer's piece sits directly beside the church's piece
in a down entry, up says the word before it is read from the bottom to the top

parts.note: a pen is a thing that writes
CE is the abbreviation for Church of England

explanation.surface: Give an author a bed beside the church for very little money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put up' reads as giving someone lodging, but 'up' turns PUT over to make TUP. Tuppence is the British word for two pence, a trifling sum.
explanation.definitionFit: Two pence is a trifling sum, used in British idiom for something that costs almost nothing.

clue.text: Suddenly collapse, seeing what fluellen wore in France?

annotationWithheld.why: Clue as held: 'Suddenly collapse, seeing what fluellen wore in France? (4)' for LEEK. Definition is 'what fluellen wore in France' (Fluellen's leek in Henry V). The only parse is 'Suddenly collapse' = KEEL OVER read as its own instruction, KEEL turned over in a down light: the one phrase supplies both the fodder KEEL and the reversal indicator OVER, so the words do two jobs and no separate clue word signals the reversal ('seeing' is a link).
annotationWithheld.clue: Suddenly collapse, seeing what fluellen wore in France?

clue.text: Bird's journey to wood at back of park

parts.note: to journey is to go
shaw is an old and dialect word for a small wood or thicket

indicators.note: back of points to the final letter of the word park

explanation.surface: A bird flies to the trees at the far side of the park.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a large, powerful hawk of northern forests, so one example of the class.

clue.text: Went round, holding up dreadful instrument

indicators.note: holding says the pieces before it wrap around the upturned word for dreadful

parts.note: went is the past of go, so it can be said as 'did go'

indicators.note: in a down entry, up says the word for dreadful is written from bottom to top

parts.note: dire means dreadful
a round shape is the letter O

explanation.surface: Someone walked about, carrying aloft a frightful musical instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went round' looks like one phrase meaning circled, but it splits into two pieces, which 'holding' wraps around the word that 'up' has turned.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an Aboriginal Australian wind instrument, a long wooden pipe giving a deep drone, so one example.

clue.text: Characteristic of little kids, some kept in in Essex

indicators.note: some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A trait of small children, a few of whom are kept indoors in an English county.
explanation.walkthrough: Essex is an English county east of London. The doubled 'in' looks like a misprint but both are needed for the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Being very small is the defining quality of young children, and this noun names that quality.

clue.text: Not quite the thing as enemy finally shell us violently

indicators.note: violently suggests the letters are thrown about by force into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word shell, which follows it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: It is bad form when the foe at last bombards us fiercely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'finally' looks as if it belongs to 'enemy', but it takes the L from 'shell'; 'violently' then rearranges ENEMY, L and US.
explanation.definitionFit: 'Not quite the thing' is an old-fashioned idiom for improper behaviour, a synonym for indecorous.

clue.text: Old girl persistently yattering about single lapse

indicators.note: about says the pieces before it go around the letter for single

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman
someone who is 'on', as in 'always on about something', keeps talking without a break
I is the Roman numeral for one, a single

explanation.surface: A former girlfriend who never stops chattering about one slip-up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like the subject of her chatter, but it is the container signal, and 'single' is a number, not her marital status.
explanation.definitionFit: A lapse is a failure to do something through oversight, a synonym for something left out.

clue.text: They casually photograph marine fish

definitions.meaning: an informal name for people who take quick, unposed photos, called snaps
a family of food fish of warm seas, the red kind being the best known

explanation.surface: Holidaymakers idly taking pictures of sea life.
explanation.definitionFit: People taking snaps are informally so called, and the same plural names a family of warm-sea food fish.

clue.text: Greeting from very excited basketball team, for example?

parts.note: someone high is elated or very excited
a basketball side has five players on court, so a five is one example of such a team

explanation.surface: A salutation from an extremely worked-up basketball side.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a celebratory slap of raised palms, used as a salute between friends or teammates.

clue.text: Recess accommodating fine blue plant

indicators.note: accommodating says the word for recess makes room inside itself for the next two pieces

parts.note: a recess is a nook or corner
F is the abbreviation for fine, as on pencil grades
blue means sad, or low in spirits

explanation.surface: An alcove with room for a lovely blue-flowered plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'blue' looks like part of the definition, and the flower is indeed that colour, but it belongs to the wordplay as a mood, placed by 'accommodating'.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a wild flower of grain fields, famous for its vivid blooms, so one example of the class.

clue.text: Resolute at labours? Not he!

indicators.note: labours suggests the letters toil and are worked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Is he determined in his work? Far from it!
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the whole clue: the person meant is the opposite of resolute at work. 'labours' rearranges RESOLUTE and AT.
explanation.definitionFit: In Homer, those who ate a certain fruit sank into idle forgetfulness, so such a person is never determined at work.

clue.text: Time in jail for one Hilary, in a word

definitions.meaning: a prison sentence, the stretch a convict serves
Hilary, for one: the name of the January-to-Easter session at Oxford University and in the English law courts
a word or expression with a particular meaning, as in a technical vocabulary

explanation.surface: A woman called Hilary sums up her prison sentence briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: Three definitions in a row. Hilary is not a woman here: it is the name of a session of the year at Oxford and in the English law courts.
explanation.definitionFit: One noun covers a prison sentence, a division of the academic or legal year such as Hilary, and any expression in a vocabulary.

clue.text: Souvenir of doctor sheltering soldiers in film

indicators.note: sheltering says the doctor's letters go around the rest, protecting it

parts.note: MO is a medical officer, a military doctor

indicators.note: in says the soldiers sit inside the title of the film

parts.note: ET is Spielberg's 1982 film, a crossword staple
men is the army word for ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A keepsake of a medic protecting troops in a movie.
explanation.definitionFit: A keepsake is an object kept as a reminder of a person or occasion, a synonym.

clue.text: Saucy mimic overcome by liquor

indicators.note: overcome by says the mimic is engulfed, surrounded by the word for liquor

parts.note: malt is malt whisky or malt liquor
an aper is one who apes or imitates, a mimic

explanation.surface: A cheeky impressionist the worse for drink.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an archaic adjective meaning impudent or cheeky, a synonym.

clue.text: In early part of day, acceptable to be wearing black

indicators.note: In, at the start, says the letter for acceptable goes inside the word for the early part of the day

parts.note: the morning is the early part of the day
U is the old British shorthand for upper-class, and so socially acceptable, usage

explanation.surface: Before noon, it is fine to be dressed in black.
explanation.walkthrough: U and non-U were 1950s British labels for upper-class and other speech, so U stands for socially acceptable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone grieving a death traditionally dresses in dark clothes, so the two describe the same state.

clue.text: Expedition leaderless group's agreed to back

indicators.note: leaderless says the word for group loses its first letter, its leader

parts.note: a body is a group of people; the possessive S stays on as a letter

indicators.note: to back says the word for agreed is written back to front

parts.note: 'Agreed!' and 'Yes!' are the same reply

explanation.surface: A trip that a party without a chief has consented to fund.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaderless' takes the B from BODY'S, leaving ODYS; 'to back' turns YES into SEY. On the surface 'back' means to finance.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a long eventful journey, named after the Greek hero's ten-year voyage home, so a synonym.

clue.text: Woman consuming instant dessert

indicators.note: consuming says the woman's name swallows the short word for an instant

parts.note: Selina is a woman's name
a mo is a moment, as in 'half a mo'

explanation.surface: A lady eating a quick-mix pudding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'instant' looks like an adjective for the pudding, but it is the noun: a MO is a moment. This is a milk pudding familiar from British school dinners.
explanation.definitionFit: It is coarse wheat cooked with milk into a pudding, a staple of British school dinners, so an example.

clue.text: Part of phone made by Wyatt that's used around city

parts.note: Wyatt Earp was the Wild West lawman of the gunfight at the OK Corral

indicators.note: used around says the letters for that's are placed round the letters for the city

parts.note: ie, short for id est, means 'that is'
EC is the postcode area of the City of London, the financial district

explanation.surface: A handset component built by Wyatt and used all over town.
explanation.walkthrough: The City, with a capital C, is London's financial district, whose postcodes carry the two letters that 'used around' encloses.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the component of a telephone handset held against the head for listening.

clue.text: Veg served where Tennyson's lady was spoken of

indicators.note: spoken of says the place name is said, not read, giving a word with the same sound

parts.note: Tennyson's poem The Lady of Shalott sets her on the island of Shalott

explanation.surface: Vegetables dished up in the place where the poet's heroine was mentioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennyson's poem is The Lady of Shalott; 'spoken of' asks for a word that sounds like her island.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a small mild onion, a kitchen vegetable, so one example.

clue.text: On turning up, speakers are vulgar

definitions.meaning: hi-fi speakers with the volume turned up are noisy
tastelessly showy, as of a garish tie or checked suit

explanation.surface: When the public orators arrive they turn out to be coarse.
explanation.definitionFit: Hi-fi speakers turned up are noisy, and a garish, tasteless thing is described by the same adjective.

clue.text: Does she half-train learner, smothered in flattery?

indicators.note: smothered in says those pieces are covered over by the word for flattery

parts.note: smarm is oily, ingratiating flattery

indicators.note: half- says only one half of the childish word for a train is used

parts.note: choo-choo is a child's word for a train
L is the learner driver's plate on British cars

explanation.surface: Is she a teacher who only partly coaches a pupil, burying them in praise?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also serves as a teasing description of the woman. The train is a child's word for one, cut by 'half-' and then 'smothered in' the flattery.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue teasingly describes a woman teacher, who does train learners; 'she' points at her.

clue.text: Arrangement of locks resorted to in play

indicators.note: resorted, read as re-sorted, says the letters that follow are sorted again into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A set of door fastenings that a stage drama falls back on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resorted' reads as 'had recourse', but as re-sorted it rearranges TO, IN and PLAY. The locks are hair, not door fastenings.
explanation.definitionFit: Locks are tresses of hair, and this is a hairstyle with the hair gathered and tied at the back.

clue.text: Small nail some doctors deal with

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a pin is a small thin nail or fastener

explanation.surface: A little fingernail that certain physicians treat.
explanation.walkthrough: The doctors are not medics: political press advisers who slant the news are called by a name ending in 'doctors'.
explanation.definitionFit: Political press advisers are nicknamed doctors of slanted presentation, so that slant is their stock in trade.

clue.text: Unbalanced Greek character standing for area used by rich

indicators.note: standing for says the Greek letter takes the place of the letter for area

parts.note: loaded is slang for very rich
psi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A deranged Greek person representing the district frequented by the wealthy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'standing for' swaps the A (area) in LOADED for PSI. 'Unbalanced' suggests a deranged person, but it means uneven.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that leans or weighs more heavily to one side is uneven, a synonym.

clue.text: A farm manager administered business, employing woman

parts.note: someone who ran an organisation administered it

indicators.note: employing says the word for business takes the woman's word on, inside itself

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a business
her is the pronoun for a woman

explanation.surface: The boss of a farm managed the firm and hired a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the Spanish-derived word for someone who owns or runs a cattle spread in Mexico or the American Southwest.

clue.text: Tone a posh girl displayed in a Cornish castle

parts.note: a tint is a shade or tone of colour
gel is how the British upper classes are supposed to pronounce girl

explanation.surface: The manner a well-bred young lady showed inside a castle in Cornwall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tone' looks like a manner of speaking but is a shade of colour. Cornwall is the county at England's south-western tip.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a ruined clifftop fortress on the north coast of Cornwall, linked in legend with King Arthur.
